opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it started as a fun internal debate, and it turned into something that says a lot about who we are as a team.

We had a few guiding principles. First, we wanted the names to reflect the kind of mathematics we care about, especially the people who changed how mathematics is *done*, not only what was proven. At Axiom we're building AI that can reason formally and verify its own work, so mathematicians who pushed toward rigor, abstraction, and new foundations felt especially meaningful to us. People who reshaped the language of mathematics, who made it possible to see deep structure across fields, are exactly the spirit we want an AI mathematician to have.

Second, we cared a lot about diversity, across eras, geographies, and backgrounds. Mathematics is a truly global, human endeavor. We wanted someone walking into a room to be reminded that great ideas came from a self-taught genius in India, from women who did foundational work when the institutions wouldn't even give them a proper title, and from people working far outside the traditional centers. That matters to me personally, too. I grew up in China, came to math through competitions, and it meant a lot to see role models who didn't fit a single mold.

Third, and this is a bit nerdy, we liked names with a story. Mathematicians who had a radical vision, who maybe weren't fully appreciated in their time, or whose ideas only became fully usable decades later. That resonates with what we're doing: betting that formal, machine-checkable mathematics will become central, even if today it still feels a bit niche.

And finally, everyone on the team got a vote. So some rooms reflect very personal favorites. Someone fell in love with a particular theorem in college and lobbied hard for its author. I think that's the nicest part: every room name is a small piece of someone's own mathematical journey.

r001.rationale: The response says the team valued mathematicians who revealed deep structure across fields and describes that as the spirit they want their AI mathematician to have.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it started as something playful and then became a kind of statement about who we are. We're an AI-for-math company, and I didn't want the rooms to just be named after the usual suspects, the names everyone already puts on buildings. I wanted each one to represent a different way that mathematics gets done, because that's actually what we're trying to teach a machine to do.

So we have a Ramanujan room, and that one is about intuition, about results arriving almost before the proof does. Ramanujan would write down formulas in his notebooks with no derivation, and it took decades for people to verify them. That tension between conjecture and proof is at the heart of what we work on every day, because a model can also produce a beautiful-looking claim that turns out to be wrong, and the hard part is checking it rigorously.

Then there's a Noether room, because Emmy Noether represents structure and abstraction, finding the right framework so that whole classes of problems become easy. That's the opposite style from Ramanujan, and I wanted both in the building.

We also have a room named after Grothendieck, and that one is partly a joke on ourselves, because his approach was to generalize until the problem dissolves. Sometimes in a meeting someone will say, "Okay, we're doing a Grothendieck right now," and that means we've gone too abstract and need to come back to the actual bug.

And then a couple were personal. There's an Euler room because he was, in a sense, the first computational mathematician. He computed relentlessly, and he was happy to use whatever worked. And we have a Hua Luogeng room, partly because of my own background and partly because he was someone who was largely self-taught and cared a lot about making mathematics useful and accessible to people. That matters to us, because the whole point of building these tools is that mathematics shouldn't be bottlenecked on a few hundred people in the world.

So the short answer is diversity of mathematical temperament. If you walked into every room and read the name, you'd get a map of the different modes of thinking we want our systems, and frankly our team, to be capable of.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the room names represent diverse mathematical temperaments and the modes of thinking it wants its systems to handle. It does not clearly connect the choices to building an AI mathematician competent across mathematical fields.

sol-6.1.text: We wanted the names to reflect the kind of thinking we value: curiosity, creativity, and a willingness to tackle difficult problems. So the idea was to celebrate mathematicians whose work inspires us, and to make those rooms a small reminder of that spirit.

r001.rationale: The response says the names were meant to celebrate inspiring mathematicians and reflect valued traits, but it does not connect choosing mathematical polymaths to an aspiration to build an AI mathematician competent across fields.
